title: They bought this N.S. bungalow as a fixer-upper. It was just demolished without their knowledge
summary: A bungalow nestled on the outskirts of Springhill, N.S., was a pandemic purchase for a couple, but they were surprised to return this fall to find all buildings and irreplaceable mementoes on the…

image.caption: The couple installed a new roof and put a fresh coat of paint on the door of the home, but after two years away the grass was overgrown. (Municipality of Cumberland)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

A bungalow nestled on the outskirts of Springhill, N.S., was a pandemic purchase for a couple, but they were surprised to return this fall to find all buildings and irreplaceable mementoes on the property gone.
Staff in northern N.S. county left notices, but owners were away for more than 2 years

A bungalow nestled on the outskirts of Springhill, N.S., was a pandemic purchase with potential for a first-generation Canadian couple, but they were surprised to return to Nova Scotia this fall to find their buildings and irreplaceable mementoes gone.
Ksenia Sabouloua and Phil Karounos bought the 4.8-hectare property sight unseen for just over $30,000 in July 2020.
The couple has worked in Ontario and the Northwest Territories but had never been to Nova Scotia, let alone the former coal mining community in Cumberland County.
The bungalow was a fixer-upper, but Sabouloua and her partner Karounos saw potential for starting a small farm.
“The East Coast was just somewhere that I always wanted to live. It's just so beautiful,” said Sabouloua in an interview.

Karounos said the home was ready for electrical fixtures and kitchen cabinets, but they ran out of money. He said the work they did to that point included shingling the roof, rewiring the home and installing a new subfloor — estimating they spent up to $30,000 on the renovations.
They didn't have enough money to finish the project all at once, and found better-paying jobs outside of Nova Scotia to help save for more renovations.
In October, they returned to the fixer-upper for the first time in more than two years.
Demolition order
To their surprise, all that was left was a muddy lot.
They found utility lines sticking up from the ground, a compost bin and pieces of debris strewn about the property.
“It was just shocking to come home. Right. That's our home no matter what,” Sabouloua said.
In August, the Municipality of Cumberland council voted to issue a demolition order for the home and a camper located on the property. The work was completed by early September.
Sabouloua said the most heartbreaking loss is not financial, but deeply personal family items stored in a shed that was also demolished.
“Pictures from Russia where I was born. All the way to my Carleton graduation diploma. So, like, just when I'm saying everything … I don't have anything,” she said, choking back tears.

In his presentation at council, director of protective services Allen Cole said the couple did not respond to notices posted on the door of the bungalow and letters mailed to another address about the potential demolition.
PHOTOS | A vacant lot is all that remains of this fixer-upper:
The staff report showed images of a hole in the side of the home and no subfloor.
Karounos said a new patio door installed in the house was also removed.
The report also said the camper was trashed on the inside.
The couple said that is not how they left it in June 2024.

“I just can't understand how this was fair. We were the victims of crime. There was obvious vandalism and all these other things, and also that there seems to be no response from the RCMP,” said Korounos.
Multiple neighbours told CBC News people were squatting at the property while the couple was away.
They also said the home was severely vandalized earlier this year — something the couple said they were not aware of until informed by the CBC.
Complaint to police
Nova Scotia RCMP said officers attended the property once in the past two years.

In June 2026, a complaint was received about the camper’s proximity to the road. Officers reported there were indications someone was living there and photographs were sent to the county through email.

“Officers confirmed through property records that the owner's listed address was in Ontario. The information forwarded to the municipality related to concerns about the condition of the property and potential safety issues observed by officers,” said an RCMP spokesperson in a statement.
The couple admit that their address was out of date but question why officials did not make more of an effort to get in touch with them.

Ksenia Sabouloua and partner Phil Karounos spent more than $50,000 to buy and fix up a small home in Springhill, N.S. After a stint away working, the couple returned to continue the project only to find it demolished. (Toni Choueiri/CBC)
Korounos said his current email address is the same one he used to communicate with the county permitting department in 2021.
The home was also slated for tax sale in October — something the couple said was an oversight on their part.
In that case Sabouloua said the county communicated with her bank who in turn contacted her. But by the time the back taxes were paid on Sept. 24, the home had already been gone for weeks.
Complaint driven

Allen Cole, who oversees dangerous or unsightly premises at the county, told CBC News he could not speak to the couple's specific order because it could become subject to litigation, such as a judicial review.

In an interview, Cole said staff do title searches and in some cases attempt to find property owners on social media. He said county records show just shy of 10 per cent of demolition orders issued have unresponsive property owners.

blocks.text: “Unless there is an issue of immediate danger, we only deal with properties for which we have received a complaint from the public,” said Cole.

“The cases are not brought to council lightly. There's significant due diligence put into every single one of these cases,” he said, noting there's been an average of about one demolition order per month since 2024.
Cole said the cost of the demolition is added to the property owner's next annual tax bill.

Sabouloua said they have no idea what that bill will be, and are still sorting out what to do next. She said it is shocking to learn how quickly the county's demolition order came after the police received a complaint, and yet they heard nothing until it was too late.
"We would have started to resolve this right away. Even if everything was stolen and the door was gone," she said.
"I would have loved to have finished it up."
